title: Out of Time
full_review:
"Out of Time" (MGM) is a tautly paced crime thriller about a small town Florida cop investigating a double homicide in which all evidence points to him as the prime suspect. Despite the film's morally clouded ending, director Carl Franklin navigates the plot turns and twists with workmanlike efficiency, resulting in an engaging neo-noir tale of lust, greed and deception.

Denzel Washington plays Matt Lee Whitlock, the chief of police in Banyan County, a lazy one-seahorse town taking up beachfront real estate in the glitzy shadow of Miami. A big fish in a small pond, Whitlock takes pride in walking his beat -- a beat that includes the bedroom of Ann Merai Harrison (Sanaa Lathan), his former high school sweetheart and the town's current abused-wife-looking-for-some-action-on-the-side. Ann's bullying, ex-quarterback husband (Dean Cain) keeps the stiffs on ice at the local morgue -- that is, when he's not treating his wife like a punching bag.

Whitlock's trouble starts as soon as he finds out that Ann has been diagnosed with an aggressive form of inoperable cancer. After Ann is told by her doctor that she has only months to live, Whitlock decides to "borrow" $400,000 of confiscated dirty money from the police station's evidence vault -- money tagged for use by the Drug Enforcement Agency to prosecute a major drug trafficker -- in order to pay for an experimental cancer treatment for Ann that might offer some slim hope of success.

But the best-laid plans usually go awry -- especially in films involving illicit trysts set in the steamy Florida Keys. The day after giving Ann the duffle bag full of cash, Whitlock is called to an arson scene which turns out to be Ann's house, containing two charred remains -- presumably those of Ann and her husband.

For vague jurisdictional reasons, Whitlock's soon-to-be-ex-wife, Alex (Eva Mendez), a sultry gold shield with the Miami Police Department, is called in to oversee the double homicide case -- her only lead a nosy neighbor's eyewitness report of a "black man" suspiciously loitering about the property the previous evening. With its shaggy-dog plot twist, the film becomes a Hitchcockian chess game as Whitlock, realizing he has been set up, tries to stay one step ahead of his fellow investigators in order to keep hidden the incriminating details of his affair with Ann, including a multimillion-dollar life insurance policy naming him as the beneficiary.

As with his previous works, including "One False Move (1992) and "Devil in a Blue Dress" (1995), Franklin proves adroit in "Out of Time" at maintaining suspense and using the film's setting -- in this case a sleepy coastal town -- as a character integral to the narrative. His choice of colors and music -- a sizzling blend of salsa and jazz -- adds to the overall moodiness, serving as visual and aural cues to the inner passions fueling the characters' infidelities and deceptions.

Whitlock is presented as a fundamentally decent, though not wholly innocent, man who uses a dubious ends-justifies-the-means reasoning to rationalize his initial misstep -- stealing the money -- which snowballs into an avalanche of lies. In one sense, Whitlock is a victim of his own moral weakness and good intentions. Yet the road to hell -- or at least the slammer -- is paved with good intentions. Whitlock's decency does not preclude his guilt.

Viewers should not overlook the fact that most of his troubles are brought on by freely choosing morally misguided courses of action. It needs also to be pointed out that Whitlock's desire to right his mistakes is not so much driven by recognizing the error of his ways, as it is by fear of being caught. He is like the boy who barely escaped getting caught with his hand in the cookie jar and who spends the rest of the day cleaning up all the crumbs.

From its opening shot -- a pan down from a neon bar sign flashing the word "temptation" -- the filmmaker clues viewers to the central theme he has chosen to explore. And while the narrative does impart an oh-what-a-tangled-web-we-weave message cautioning viewers to the consequences of deception, it does so by making its hero an adulterous thief who -- at least for much of the film -- seems to care more about saving his own skin than pursuing justice. Whitlock's dishonesty is compounded by that of his friend, the town coroner (John Billingsley), who helps cover his boss' tracks with still more lies. Like Whitlock's escape act, his deceits are winked at approvingly, even applauded. Ultimately, viewers are asked to root against the system, which Whitlock beats without recrimination. For that, "Out of Time" is morally out of line.

Due to a few sexual encounters, some violence and sporadic crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
